'''Faiza Mohammed Al-Kharafi''' ({{langx|ar|فايزة الخرافي|translit=Fāyzah al-Kharāfī}}; born 1946) is a Kuwaiti chemist and academic. She was the president of [[Kuwait University]] from 1993 to 2002, and the first woman to head a major university in the Middle East.<ref name="Forbes"/> She is the vice president of [[TWAS|the World Academy of Sciences]].

==Early life and education==
Faiza Al-Kharafi was born to a wealthy family in Kuwait in 1946 and developed an interest in science from a young age.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://cdm16639.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16639coll5/id/41|title=Dr. Faiza Al-Kharafi|website=ContentDM|access-date=31 January 2020|archive-date=31 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200131161204/https://cdm16639.contentdm.oclc.org/digital/collection/p16639coll5/id/41|url-status=live}}</ref> She attended Al Merkab High School. She received her BSc from [[Ain Shams University]] in Cairo in 1967. She then attended [[Kuwait University]] where she founded the Corrosion and Electrochemistry Research Laboratory while in graduate school. She received her master's in 1972 and her PhD in 1975.<ref name="Who"/>

==Career==
Al-Kharafi worked in Kuwait University's Department of Chemistry from 1975 to 1981. In 1984 she became chair of the department and was Dean of the Faculty of Science from 1986 to 1989.<ref name="Who">{{cite web|title=Fayza Al Khorafi |url=http://www.whoswhoarabwomen.com/profiles.asp?a=307 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130624234519/http://www.whoswhoarabwomen.com/profiles.asp?a=307 |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 June 2013 |publisher=Who's Who Amongst Arab Women |access-date=20 June 2013 }}</ref> She became a professor of chemistry at Kuwait University in 1987.<ref>{{cite book|last=O'Shea|first=Maria|title=Kuwait|year=1999|publisher=Marshall Cavendish Corp.|location=New York|isbn=978-0-7614-0871-0|page=[https://archive.org/details/kuwait00oshe/page/61 61]|url=https://archive.org/details/kuwait00oshe|url-access=registration|quote=Faiza Al-Kharafi sunni.|edition=2nd}}</ref> On 5 July 1993, Emir [[Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah]] issued a decree appointing Al-Kharafi as rector of the university,<ref name=KUNA>{{cite web|title=This day of Kuwait's history|url=http://www.kuna.net.kw/ArticleDetails.aspx?id=2012111&language=en|publisher=[[Kuwait News Agency]]|date=5 July 2009|access-date=20 June 2013|archive-date=27 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927170736/http://www.kuna.net.kw/ArticleDetails.aspx?id=2012111&language=en|url-status=live}}</ref> and she became the first woman to head a major university in the Middle East.<ref name="Forbes"/> Al-Kharafi helped reconstruct Kuwait University after the First Gulf War, which ended in 1991. She was president from 1993 to 2002, where she oversaw 1,500 staff members, over 5,000 employees, and over 20,000 students.<ref name=":0" />

Al- Kharafi has demonstrated to be an advocate for research in Kuwait. In 1986, Al- Kharafi and her colleagues explored and compared the rich development of Kuwaiti scientific research in comparison to other nations in the third world. In her publication, Al- Kharafi was able to demonstrate the ability of Kuwait's higher education institutions to engage in relevant scientific research.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Al-Kharafi|first1=Faiza|last2=El-Rayyes|first2=Nizar|last3=Janini|first3=George|date=February 1987|title=Science research in Kuwait—a bibliometric analysis|journal=Journal of Information Science|volume=13|issue=1|pages=37–44|doi=10.1177/016555158701300106|s2cid=31394410|issn=0165-5515}}</ref>

Al-Kharafi has studied the impact of [[corrosion engineering|corrosion]] on engine cooling systems, distillation units for [[crude oil]], high temperature geothermal brines, and tap water. She has also studied corrosion in polluted water and metal corrosion caused by pollution. As an electrochemist, she studied the electrochemical behavior of metals and metal alloys including aluminum, copper, platinum, niobium, vanadium, cadmium, brass, cobalt, and low carbon steel.<ref>{{cite web|title=Faiza al-Kharafi|url=http://cnre.mit.edu/people/advisory-board/al-kharafi|publisher=Kuwait–MIT Center|access-date=20 June 2013|archive-date=5 March 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305025509/http://cnre.mit.edu/people/advisory-board/al-kharafi|url-status=live}}</ref> She collaborated on the discovery of a class of [[molybdenum]]-based catalysts that improve gasoline octane without benzene by-products.<ref>{{cite news|title=Faiza Al-Kharafi (Αφρική και Αραβικές Χώρες)|url=http://www.enet.gr/?i=news.el.article&id=256396|newspaper=[[Eleftherotypia]]|date=3 March 2011|access-date=20 June 2013|archive-date=28 September 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130928022425/http://www.enet.gr/?i=news.el.article&id=256396|url-status=live|language=el}}</ref>

She joined the Board of the [[United Nations University]] in 1998.<ref name=KUNA/> Following the passage of [[women's suffrage in Kuwait]] in 2005, she said "when we have political rights, we can express our opinion and vote for the correct person... This gives us the chance to express our ideas."<ref name="Forbes"/> In 2006, she helped found the American Bilingual School in Kuwait. She is the vice president of [[TWAS|The World Academy of Sciences]]. She is on many boards, including the Kuwait Foundation for the Advancement Sciences, [[Alqabas]], the Kuwait-MIT Center for Natural Resources and the Environment.

==Awards and honours==
''[[Forbes]]'' magazine named her as one of "The 100 Most Powerful Women – Women To Watch in the Middle East" in 2005.<ref name="Forbes">{{cite web|title=Middle Eastern Women To Watch|url=https://www.forbes.com/2005/07/26/cz_05powom_middleeastern_slide.html|work=Forbes|date=26 July 2005|access-date=27 August 2017|archive-date=26 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161226150851/http://www.forbes.com/2005/07/26/cz_05powom_middleeastern_slide.html|url-status=live}}</ref> She received the Kuwait Prize in Applied Sciences in 2006. The Council for Gulf Relations named her Top Gulf Woman of the Year in 2008.<ref name="Ambassadors">{{cite news|last=Farag|first=Talaat I.|title=Dr. Faiza Al-Khorafi, PhD|url=http://ambassadors.net/archives/issue24/editorial.htm|newspaper=The Ambassadors Online Magazine|date=July 2008|access-date=20 June 2013|archive-date=10 January 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120110154621/http://ambassadors.net/archives/issue24/editorial.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> In 2011, she was the recipient of the [[L'Oréal-UNESCO Awards for Women in Science|L'Oréal-UNESCO Award for Women in Science]] for her work on corrosion.<ref>{{cite web|title=Outstanding women scientists to receive 2011 L'ORÉAL-UNESCO Awards (3 March) and Fellowships (2 March)|url=http://www.unesco.org/new/en/media-services/single-view/news/outstanding_women_scientists_to_receive_2011_loreal_unesco_awards_3_march_and_fellowships_2_march/|publisher=UNESCO|date=25 February 2011|access-date=20 June 2013|archive-date=19 August 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120819032319/http://www.unesco.org/new/en/media-services/single-view/news/outstanding_women_scientists_to_receive_2011_loreal_unesco_awards_3_march_and_fellowships_2_march|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Al-Kharafi is married to Ali Mohammed Thanian Al-Ghanim and has five sons and ten grandchildren. Of her sons, [[Marzouq Al-Ghanim]] is a former speaker of Kuwait National Assembly. She spends her Summers at [[Lake Geneva]], Switzerland. Her brothers are [[Jassem Al-Kharafi]], former speaker of the Kuwaiti National Assembly, and the late [[Nasser Al-Kharafi]]. She shares in the family fortune from [[M. A. Kharafi & Sons]].<ref name="Who"/><ref name="Ambassadors"/>
